en: And divided them in every direction.
Driving one to the faraway wilderness,
Driving one down
Into depths that could not be forded.
Driving one to Altay,
Driving one beyond Dongduk to Kanggay.
Driving one away
To the hollow of Zhelpinish,
Driving one away
Along the land of Zhet-Kayt.
There is no news, no word,
Where ears may hear but eyes cannot see,
‘They have gone to an unknown place,’ I say,
And now I despair.
‘To the true abode from which none return,
The dear children have gone,’ I thought.
I wore out horses with long travel,
To hear news of my kin,
I roamed the earth without stopping.
Finding no kin, I grew weary;
My upright work was righteous,
I have met a kinsman, Manas!
If you come migrating from Altay,
You have a migration that will not ruin your settlement.
Among the Chinese, the people of forty khans,
There is vengeance owed for many of your forefathers.
From the Black Kalmyks and Chinese,
Separate your village and make it apart.
To reach here at last in migration,
Castrate the stallions and make geldings!
If you come safely into my hands,
I will bring slaughter upon the world.
Of the Chinese of forty tribes,
I will seize their khanate!
Into the endless multitudes
I will go straight and thrust my spear.
If the enemy comes out to fight to the end,
Beneath the standard, without stirring,
I will stand holding your standard.
If you come straight into my hands,
I will raise an uproar in the world!
If you come and settle,
If you become Koshoy's support,
The one I will fight is my Kakan-Chin.
I have much vengeance against the Manchus,
I have a song to sing,
Then I have a secret to tell.
In the four corners of the circle,
I have quarrels to fight!
I have a migration coming from Altay,
I have vengeance to take where we fight,
I have a secret to speak openly.
My lion, if you come into my hands,
I have turmoil to raise in the world.
On the ridge side are the Chinese,
I have many enemies to clash with.
On the lowland side are the Russians,
I have many foes to grapple with.
Before me there are guns,
I have many enemies to contend with.
I have a secret to tell in full.
My lord, come into my hands,
I have many a quarrel to raise!
If you look, the eye cannot reach its end;
If I tell the prose tale,
Words will not suffice your elder!
The one I will fight is Kakan-Chin,
To bring upheaval—
Aykhoja's Bilerik,
From that day to this day,
Jar Manas of Samarkand,
He and Bilerik are in one place.
Of the Chinese, with iron ropes,
They stand in a net, I hear.
Deep-dug by the Chinese,
They stand in a pit, I hear.
The oppression of the Last Judgment
They are about to face, I hear.
They have lain there many years,
They are about to die, I hear.
When I remember them,
A house built off to the side,
Flaring in anger, burning within,
My wretched soul cannot fit in a fist!
For those children in torment,
For those souls under oppression,
‘I would gather my army without looking back,
Against the seething Chinese
I would bring a mighty slaughter,’ I thought.
I would thrust spears and break the ranks,
If death came, I would fall to a bullet!
I would go and camp at Beijing,
For the hero lying bound,
I would face terrible suffering,
Fighting summer and winter,
I would shed blood like water,
If death came, I would die!
Aykhoja's Bilerik
They captured on the hunt.
Jar Manas of Samarkand
They captured thinking he was you.
Having judges assess him,
They put him too into the pit!
If Jar Manas gets out alive,
Please agree to what I say:
When he comes to the Last Judgment,
Let that soul go without looking back;
Give him your younger sister!
As for giving your younger sister—
I have more words to tell,
If Jar Manas should die,
Tomorrow, on the Day of Judgment,
My sultan, his blood is upon you!
For that soul lying imprisoned,
How can I stand and endure?
While my beard is white,
While my journey draws near,
I will make war on the Chinese!
The poor man in bonds,
I will set him free!
I have twelve thousand troops,
I will sweep across their land,
Those who dwell in their courts,
I will descend upon their heads!
I will bring exceeding torment.
If Allah Most High gives aid,
The children living in humiliation,
I will set them free!
When the people move upward,
When horses' tongues darken with grass,
Then I will raise an uproar!
Shooting arrows like rain,
Firing bullets like hail,
When you yourself and the Chinese
Are fighting a slaughtering battle,
I will free you!
The span of time is six months;
Write down the days before you go,
Take the count of days with you!
Against the surging Black Chinese
I will raise turmoil.
When you yourself and the Chinese
Are struggling together,
That is exactly when I will come!
Here is another marvel to tell;
There is reason in the spoken word.
The youngest of the eight,
Karakan's foal,
There is one called Ulak Khan.
When they brought great slaughter,
When the Chinese surrounded them,
The humiliation wrought by the Chinese,
He learned of it, I heard.
Old Kayyp snatched him away,
At the edge of ancient Turpan,
Of cursed Barbar,
On its northward-pouring side,
There is no mountain the size of an ankle-bone,
No hollow the size of a saddlecloth,
Beside the Lop River,
Beyond it, at the forest's edge,
A great people whose battle cry is Kyrgyz,
They are a people named Noygut.
The one who rules those Noygut
Is a khan called Karacha.
To Karacha's people,
He knew they had become enemies.
‘Let offspring of the khan remain,’ he thought,
And brought him in there.
‘An entrusted charge,’ old Kayyp said,
And gave him to Karacha.
Karacha, khan of the Noygut,
Was a man of sacred power.
‘From Khan Karakan, the falcon,
A gift left behind,’ he said,
‘Of such a falcon,
We need a child,’ he said.
When they brought and gave the child,
They slaughtered ninety mares for his feast.
The people rejoiced and called out,
Scattered treasure and held a feast.
Many people gathered,
They bestowed great honor, they say.
That poor Ulak Khan,
Giving him the name Ulak Khan,
They took him as an honored ward, they say.
They agreed to what he said, they say.
In a red dress, with a moonlike waist,
From among the swaying beauties,
They found him a wife, they say.
Keeping a court, becoming khan,
Becoming a steady man,
His drunkenness from drinking kumys,
His youth with its unruly ways,
All vanished completely.
In Karacha's city,
He prospered as a sultan,
Kept a san of livestock and grew rich,
He lives in happiness, I hear.
‘Is there news of my kin?’
Of those who come and go,
He keeps asking, I hear.
He is a stalwart, he is a hero,
My hero, to you yourself,
He is the lion who will be a companion!
The course of a dug channel,
The offspring of a prince!
If you go out in front, he is your support.
My child, for you yourself,
He is the hero who will be a companion!
‘Your kinsman Manas has come,’ I will say,
I will give six swift horses.
To Ulak Khan himself
I will give a letter the size of a palm.
Catch and ride, my hero,
A swift steed chosen from the herd.
Against the seething Chinese,
When we wage a crushing war,
I will bring along with me
Such a kinsman as Ulak Khan.
He is the support to put your trust in.
If you mark him well, my foal,
Ulak Khan, born valiant,
He is the hero to bind about your waist,
He is a man of mighty ancestral spirit.
The youngest of eight sons,
A servant of the one God,
He is the hero who will be your companion!
His bravery is known to the people,
Both a kinsman and a hero,
For you yourself, lion Manas,
A supporting kinsman not easily found!
With broad skirts and a generous heart,
Broad shoulders fit for a hero,
Both blessed and fortunate,
Now he burns with longing!
Your support before you,
The king's Ulak Khan,
Your close protector!
Both a wrestler and a hero,
Such is the nature of Ulak Khan—
A sage full of wisdom!
If Ulak Khan comes into your hands,
He is the steep path, he is the mountain pass!
For my dark slanting path where dogs perish,
He is the hero who will prove his worth!
Here is a fine thing to tell,
My lion Manas, listen!
Heed my words, please go back.
From the hands of the forty Chinese tribes,
Akbaltay, khan of the Kyrgyz,
Please set him free!
When you have come this way,
Of the Kyrgyz, forty households,
Let the Black Chinese and the many Manchus
Not descend upon their heads,
